query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, stress–strain behavior, thermal expansion, and elastic behavior at elevated temperatures remain insufficiently understood. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain these responses? Define a controlled comparison, the observations predicted relative to a baseline state, the temperature and response limits within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: At elevated temperatures, the HfNbTaTiZr refractory HEA undergoes a stress‐induced local ordering transition that alters its elastic and thermal expansion behavior by modifying dislocation mobility and lattice anharmonicity.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase, homogeneously disordered BCC HfNbTaTiZr alloy at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Heat the alloy to temperatures between approximately 600°C and 1000°C while applying controlled uniaxial tensile and compressive loads under quasi-static conditions.
generation.conditions: The tests should be conducted in a controlled environment within the 600–1000°C range and under loading rates that allow atomic rearrangements to occur. Room-temperature measurements serve as the baseline.
generation.structural_mediator: Stress- and temperature-activated formation of short-range ordered atomic clusters.
generation.mechanism: Thermal activation enables local atomic rearrangements under stress, leading to the formation of short-range order. This local reordering modifies the effective elastic moduli and alters dislocation mobility, which in turn influences both the stress–strain response and the thermal expansion behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline (room-temperature, fully disordered state), samples tested at 600–1000°C will exhibit increased elastic anisotropy, non-linear temperature-dependent thermal expansion, and anomalous yield behavior that correlate with the onset of local atomic ordering (detectable with in situ diffraction techniques).
generation.baseline: Mechanical and thermal properties measured at room temperature, where the alloy is in a fully disordered state.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold under quasi-static loading within the 600–1000°C temperature window. Outside this range (e.g., below 600°C or under dynamic loading conditions), the ordering transition may not activate, and the associated modulations of mechanical behavior may not be observed.
generation.uncertainty: The exact temperature onset and extent of the ordering transition, as well as the magnitude of its effect on mechanical properties, are uncertain and may depend on processing history and microstructural variations.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct in situ high-temperature neutron diffraction concurrently with uniaxial tensile and compressive stress–strain testing of HfNbTaTiZr samples heated from 600°C to 1000°C. Simultaneously monitor thermal expansion and elastic moduli. Compare the evolution of diffraction patterns for signs of local ordering against the mechanical response.
measurements: In situ diffraction data to track short-range ordering
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, within the temperature range of 600–1000°C, no discernible change in the diffraction patterns indicating local ordering is observed despite significant changes in elastic or thermal expansion behavior, then the hypothesis—that the mechanical and thermal anomalies are driven by stress-induced local atomic ordering—will be falsified.

Temperature dependence of elastic and plastic deformation behavior of a refractory high-entropy alloy

Abstract: The present work discovers the unique deformation behavior of a refractory high-entropy alloy at elevated temperatures. Single-phase solid-solution refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) show remarkable mechanical properties, such as their high yield strength and substantial softening resistance at elevated temperatures. Hence, the in-depth study of the deformation behavior for body-centered cubic (BCC) refractory HEAs is a critical issue to explore the uncovered/unique deformation mechanisms. We have investigated the elastic and plastic deformation behaviors of a single BCC NbTaTiV refractory HEA at elevated temperatures using integrated experimental efforts and theoretical calculations. The in situ neutron diffraction results reveal a temperature-dependent elastic anisotropic deformation behavior. The single-crystal elastic moduli and macroscopic Young’s, shear, and bulk moduli were determined from the in situ neutron diffraction, showing great agreement with first-principles calculations, machine learning, and resonant ultrasound spectroscopy results. Atomistic clustering-ordering and high-strain deformation of an Al0.1CrCoFeNi high-entropy alloy

Abstract: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments.
